# Pre-v1 audit — every concrete shape `pkg/v1` publishes by alias

**Generated by reading the tree, not by memory.** Regenerate before deciding
anything: the script is at the bottom of this file.

## Why this list exists

ADR 0039 settled the interface half: a published **port** is extended by a
sibling interface, never by widening, because Go interfaces are structural and
adding a method breaks every downstream double at compile time with no
deprecation window.

ADR 0040 settled the other half, and gave it an expiry date. A published
**concrete shape** has no sibling trick — `pkg/v1/metrics.Snapshot` is a type
alias, so when `SnapshotValue` changed form the change reached every consumer
directly. That was permitted **only because the module is v0**, said out loud in
the commit rather than left silent, and ADR 0040 states plainly that the licence
is gone at v1.

This file is the inventory that licence applies to. At v1 every shape below is
frozen against anything a semver-minor release may not break, so the list is
what has to be reviewed *before* the tag, not after.

## How to read it

The three groups are not equally expensive, and lumping them together is how
this kind of audit gets abandoned halfway.

- **Group A — construction shapes.** Callers build these, with field names, at
  a call site they own. Adding a field is safe at any version; only removing or
  retyping one breaks. Cheap.
- **Group B — value shapes returned to callers.** The SDK builds these and hands
  them over; a caller destructures them, switches on their fields, or stores
  them. Every change is observable, and even an *added* field breaks a caller
  who wrote a composite literal without field names. Expensive.
- **Group C — everything else.** Engine handles, registries, plain shapes. Read
  each: a handle whose fields are all unexported is opaque in practice and costs
  nothing to change; a plain shape is as exposed as group B.

The count that matters for planning is group B.

## Regenerating

```bash
python3 - <<'PY'
import re, io, glob
alias = {}
for f in glob.glob('pkg/v1/**/*.go', recursive=True):
    if f.endswith('_test.go'): continue
    src = io.open(f, encoding='utf-8').read()
    for m in re.finditer(r'^(?:type\s+)?([A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*)(\[[^\]]*\])?\s*=\s*([\w]+)\.([A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*)', src, re.M):
        alias.setdefault((m.group(4), m.group(3)), set()).add((f, m.group(1)))
kinds = {}
for f in glob.glob('internal/**/*.go', recursive=True):
    if f.endswith('_test.go'): continue
    for m in re.finditer(r'^type ([A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*)(\[[^\]]*\])?\s+(struct|interface|func)\b',
                         io.open(f, encoding='utf-8').read(), re.M):
        kinds.setdefault(m.group(1), set()).add(m.group(3))
for (t, p), uses in sorted(alias.items()):
    if 'struct' in kinds.get(t, ()):
        print(t, p, sorted(uses)[0][0])
PY
```

Two traps this script already fell into, recorded so the next reader does not
repeat them:

- **The aliases are written `type X = pkg.Y` on one line**, not inside a
  `type ( … )` block. A pattern anchored on the block form reports **5** structs
  instead of 124 — and 5 looks plausible enough to be believed.
- **A count is never deduced, only measured.** The first run of this audit was
  wrong by a factor of 25 and looked fine.
